questions.q: What's the difference between a workbook and a worksheet?
questions.a: A workbook is the whole Excel file. A worksheet is one grid inside it, with its own tab at the bottom. A workbook can hold many worksheets, for example one per month.
questions.listen: Correct terms, and a real example of when you'd use several sheets.
options: A workbook is the file; worksheets are the tabs inside it
A worksheet is the file; workbooks are the tabs
A workbook is a printed sheet

questions.q: What does COUNT do differently from COUNTA?
questions.a: COUNT counts cells that hold numbers. COUNTA counts every cell that isn't empty, including text. To count how many students wrote a test, use COUNT on the marks; to count names, use COUNTA.
questions.listen: The numbers-only point, and choosing the right one for a task.
options: COUNT counts numbers; COUNTA counts any non-empty cell
COUNT counts text; COUNTA counts numbers

questions.q: Explain relative and absolute references.
questions.a: A relative reference like B2 moves when you copy the formula, so each row points at its own cells. An absolute reference like $B$2 stays fixed, which you need for a single rate or total that every row uses. F4 adds the $ signs.
questions.listen: Why it matters when filling, the $ notation, and F4.
options: Relative references move when copied; absolute ($B$2) stay fixed
Absolute references only work on other sheets

questions.q: When would you use a mixed reference such as $A2 or B$1?
questions.a: When only the row or only the column should stay fixed, typically in a two-way table. In a multiplication table, =$A2*B$1 keeps column A and row 1 locked so one formula fills the whole grid.
questions.listen: A concrete two-way example.
options: For two-way tables where one part must stay fixed

questions.q: A colleague's sheet shows #####. What's wrong?
questions.a: Usually nothing is wrong with the value: the column is too narrow to show the number or date. Widen the column, or double-click the column border to AutoFit.
questions.listen: That it's a display issue, not a formula error.

questions.q: What do #DIV/0!, #NAME? and #VALUE! tell you?
questions.a: #DIV/0! means dividing by zero or an empty cell. #NAME? means Excel doesn't recognise a word, usually a typo in a function name. #VALUE! means maths on text, like a number stored with "kg" after it.
questions.listen: Each error mapped to its cause, and fixing the cause rather than hiding it.
options: They all mean the same thing
Divide by zero; unknown name; maths on text
Too narrow; deleted cell; wrong date
Protected sheet; wrong password; old file

questions.q: How do you keep the header row visible while scrolling a long list?
questions.a: View › Freeze Panes › Freeze Top Row. To freeze rows and columns together, click the cell just below and right of what should stay, then View › Freeze Panes.
questions.listen: Freeze Panes, and knowing it's a screen setting (printing uses Print Titles).

questions.q: Why do many teams avoid Merge & Center?
questions.a: Merged cells break sorting, filtering, copying columns and keyboard selection. Center Across Selection (Ctrl+1 › Alignment) gives the same look without merging.
questions.listen: The practical problems, and the alternative.
options: Merged cells break sorting and selecting; use Center Across Selection

questions.q: What makes a list "clean" enough for Excel's tools?
questions.a: One header row, one record per row, no blank rows or columns inside, one fact per cell, numbers stored as numbers and dates as dates, and no subtotal rows in the middle.
questions.listen: Several of these rules, especially no blank rows and one fact per cell.
options: One header row, no gaps, one fact per cell

questions.q: What are the benefits of an Excel Table (Ctrl+T)?
questions.a: A Table grows automatically when you add rows, fills formulas down by itself, has filter buttons and banding, supports readable formulas like =SUM(Sales[Amount]), and adds a Total Row that follows filters.
questions.listen: Auto-expanding ranges and structured references.
options: They grow with new rows and use readable references

questions.q: How do you sort by region, then by amount within each region?
questions.a: Click a cell in the data, open Data › Sort, sort by Region A to Z, click Add Level, then sort by Amount largest to smallest. Make sure My data has headers is ticked.
questions.listen: Data › Sort with levels, and not selecting just one column.
options: Sort Region, then sort Amount with the A-Z button

questions.q: How would you stop people typing the wrong category in a column?
questions.a: Data validation with a List: select the cells, Data › Data Validation, Allow: List, and point the Source at the list of allowed values. Add a clear error message.
questions.listen: Data validation, a source range, and helpful messages.

questions.q: How do you protect formulas but still let people type inputs?
questions.a: Every cell is locked by default but it only matters once the sheet is protected. Unlock the input cells (Ctrl+1 › Protection), then Review › Protect Sheet.
questions.listen: The two-step order: unlock inputs, then protect.
options: Unlock the inputs, then protect the sheet

questions.q: A total looks too low but shows no error. What might be happening?
questions.a: Some numbers may be stored as text, which SUM skips silently. Look for numbers sitting on the left and green triangles, then convert them to numbers. Also check the SUM range covers every row.
questions.listen: Text numbers and checking the range, for example with the status bar.
options: Numbers stored as text, or a range that misses rows

questions.q: How would you show 12500000 as 1,25,00,000?
questions.a: Use a number format with Indian grouping: Currency or Accounting with ₹ English (India), or the custom format #,##,##0. The value stays 12500000; only the look changes.
questions.listen: That formats change the display, not the value.

questions.q: Which keyboard shortcuts save you the most time?
questions.a: For example Ctrl+Arrow to jump to the edge of data, Ctrl+Shift+Arrow to select to the edge, F4 to lock references, Ctrl+1 for Format Cells, Ctrl+T for a Table, Alt+= for AutoSum, and Ctrl+` to show formulas.
questions.listen: Specific shortcuts and what they're for.

questions.q: How do you print a wide, long report so it's readable?
questions.a: Switch to Landscape, set Scale to Fit Width to 1 page with Height on Automatic, repeat the header row with Print Titles, add page numbers in the footer, and check with Ctrl+P.
questions.listen: Fit to width (not the whole sheet on one page) and Print Titles.
options: Fit the sheet on one page
Landscape, fit width to 1 page, repeat headers

questions.q: What's the fill handle for, and what is Flash Fill?
questions.a: The fill handle copies a formula or continues a series (Jan, Feb, Mar…) as you drag it. Flash Fill (Ctrl+E) spots a pattern from an example you type, like splitting first names from full names.
questions.listen: Series and formulas for the fill handle; pattern by example for Flash Fill.
options: Fill handle copies and continues series; Flash Fill copies a pattern you show it

questions.q: What does =2+3*4 give, and why?
questions.a: 14. Excel follows the order of operations: multiplication before addition, so 3*4 is 12, then 2 is added. Use brackets, =(2+3)*4, to get 20.
questions.listen: The answer and the rule (BODMAS).

questions.q: How do you check that someone else's formulas are right?
questions.a: Show Formulas (Ctrl+`) to spot typed numbers among formulas, press F2 on a formula to see the ranges it uses, and compare totals with the status bar Sum of the selected cells.
questions.listen: Several concrete checks, not just "I look at it".
options: Ctrl+`, F2 and the status bar
